entry.title: T3 Code: one control surface for all your coding agents
entry.content:
Claude Code in one terminal, Codex in another, Cursor somewhere else: the agents are good, the way we juggle them is not. T3 Code (MIT, ~56k GitHub stars) attacks exactly that gap, and it is careful about what it claims to be.

Not a harness🔗

The README calls it an agent harness control surface. The nuance is real: T3 Code gives no tools to any model and runs nothing itself. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity and others already do that. T3 Code spawns those CLIs, wraps them in a proper interface, and lets you reach them remotely. Your subscription stays yours; T3 is free, and there is nothing to buy.

What you get🔗

  • Every client: Electron desktop app, web app (app.t3.codes), iOS and Android.
  • Remote first: agents run on the machine hosting the server. t3 up exposes it through T3 Connect, LAN pairing or Tailscale. Close the laptop, the VPS or desktop keeps working, and the phone is just a remote.
  • Permission modes, per thread: Supervised, Auto-accept edits, Auto, Full access. Subagent requests land in the parent conversation.
  • Worktrees to isolate each task, plus a cleanup screen, because they eat disk fast.

Install🔗

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
t3

Also available via Homebrew (t3-code cask), the AUR (t3code-bin), winget, scoop and nixpkgs.

Before you commit🔗

  • It is early: expect bugs, and big contributions are not accepted yet.
  • No local models, by deliberate choice.
  • Claude runs through Anthropic’s Agent SDK: the 5-hour limit drains faster than with Claude Code directly. Weekly limits are unaffected, and the bug is on Anthropic’s side.
  • Code goes to your provider, not to T3 servers. Telemetry is product usage only and can be turned off.
  • T3 Connect is free for three machines; more requires a paid T3 Chat plan, unless you self-host or use Tailscale.

Verdict🔗

T3 Code does not make your agents smarter. It makes them reachable, comparable and properly supervised, which is most of what daily agent work actually needs. If you juggle two harnesses or want to prompt from the couch, it is the best free option I have tried. If you live happily in a single CLI, your terminal is still fine.

entry.title: ThinkRail: JetBrains builds a real IDE around the pi coding agent
entry.content:
There is a moment, after a few weeks of vibe coding in a terminal, when you notice you are no longer programming. You are watching a transcript scroll, scrolling back to figure out which file the agent touched, and typing git diff in a panic. The agent is fine. Your workflow is not.

ThinkRail is JetBrains’ answer to that. It is an agentic IDE: a real editor, a real terminal, a real diff viewer, wrapped around the pi coding agent. It comes from the JetBrains InnovationHub incubator, not from the IntelliJ team, and it is open source (Apache-2.0), free, and account-less. That last part matters more than it sounds: no login, no seat, no telemetry-driven upsell for the app itself.

What ThinkRail actually is🔗

ThinkRail is not an IntelliJ plugin, and it is not another fork of VS Code. It is a thin host: the pi engine runs in-process inside ThinkRail and owns the hard parts (models, skills, context compaction, token cost, session state). ThinkRail owns everything around it: workspaces, the GUI, and the typed contract between the engine and the UI.

Under the hood, the architecture is refreshingly boring, in the best sense:

  • an HTTP + WebSocket host (Bun) with one pi session per chat;
  • a versioned, typed protocol between host and UI;
  • a React web client, shipped independently;
  • two front-ends for the same engine: a native desktop app (packaged with Electrobun) and a thinkrail CLI that opens the same UI in your browser.

Because it is a host, ThinkRail never assembles prompts behind your back. Your ~/.pi configuration is the source of truth: providers, models, skills, extensions, chat history. You can start a session in ThinkRail and continue it from the pi CLI, or the other way round. This is the opposite of the usual vendor lock-in play, and it is the single most important design decision in the product.

Workspaces: agents deserve worktrees, not your working tree🔗

The core idea is simple: a project is any local git repo, and a workspace is a git worktree cut from it. Each workspace gets its own branch, its own working directory, its own files, terminals, diffs and chats.

In practice, you click “Start building”, pick a base branch, write a description (which doubles as the first prompt), and the agent starts working in ~/.thinkrail/worktrees/<project>/workspace-1. Your checkout is untouched. If the agent rewrites a file, deletes something, or runs a formatter you did not ask for, the damage is contained to that branch. You merge what you like and delete the rest.

The consequence everyone underestimates: parallelism becomes safe. Three agents on three worktrees cannot fight over the same files, because they are not in the same directory. One can refactor a module while another rewrites the specs, and neither will discover a half-written file from the other.

Small details that show the feature was actually used: workspaces that are finished park themselves on a Settled shelf when their PR merges or closes, or after a configurable idle period (one, three, seven or fourteen days, or never); and they come back the moment you touch them again.

Spec-driven development, without the ceremony🔗

The second pillar is the spec graph. Every module can carry a SPEC.md file with a YAML header that links it to the others:

---
id: module-server
type: module-design
status: active
parent: architecture
depends-on: [goal-and-requirements]
tags: [engine, contracts]
---

The status field alone (draft, active, stale, done, deprecated) is worth the price of admission: a spec cannot silently rot, because its staleness is written down. At the root of the repo you keep goal-and-requirements.md and architecture.md; below, one SPEC.md per genuine module.

The crucial part is not the format, it is who maintains it. ThinkRail bundles a pi-spec-graph extension that gives the agent dedicated spec_* tools to search, navigate and update the graph. When a change moves a boundary or breaks a contract, the spec is supposed to be updated in the same turn, never after. The agent reads the nearest spec instead of the whole codebase, which keeps its context small and its answers grounded.

This is Spec-Driven Development as JetBrains frames it: documentation comes back not because managers asked for it, but because it is the cheapest way to keep an agent on course across sessions. The specs are the guardrails — always present, never in the way when things go well.

The IDE part is not decorative🔗

A chat panel is not an IDE. ThinkRail ships the boring, indispensable pieces:

  • Monaco tabs (the VS Code editor engine), with syntax highlighting, rendered Markdown and a source toggle;
  • a file tree scoped to the active worktree, with a changed-files filter;
  • a git changes panel that diffs the workspace branch live, while the agent is still typing;
  • real PTYs, so you can run your tests yourself while the agent keeps working;
  • a review panel where you collect line comments and send them back to the agent in one message.

The review flow is the feature I did not expect to care about. When a turn changes files, it ends with a receipt like 3 files changed · +27 −4 and a Review turn button. Those numbers do not come from the agent’s own claims: the host snapshots the worktree at the start and at the end of the run, so a formatter or a shell sed counts too. You then read everything in one scroll, with Keep, Revert, and Ask agent about this hunk on each hunk, and J to jump to the next unreviewed file. Keep is keyed to the hunk content, so it survives line shifts.

That single design change — review the turn, not the chat log — is what turns an agent from a toy into a colleague.

Chat, models, and the small things that matter🔗

The chat is built for real work rather than demos:

  • several concurrent sessions per workspace, each with its own model and reasoning effort;
  • you can steer a running turn or queue a follow-up instead of waiting for the agent to finish;
  • live token accounting: input, output, cache reads and writes, cost, and how full the context window is;
  • a plan shared between you and the agent, with a full page showing each finished step’s summary and verification;
  • background resources (commands, subagents, MCP servers) in one popup;
  • ⌘K / Ctrl+K / double-tap Shift opens one box that finds chats and messages inside them, workspaces, projects, files, specs and plans, runs app commands, and — when empty — lists every chat waiting on you across all projects. That last trick fixes the real bottleneck of parallel agents: noticing which one is blocked on a question.
  • interactive tools: the agent can ask you structured multiple-choice questions in the chat instead of guessing, draw Mermaid diagrams, and show before/after mockups you can comment on like a diff.

On the model side, ThinkRail has no accounts of its own. You sign in with JetBrains AI or connect any provider through pi’s auth. You can also point it at a company gateway or a local model server — Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM, sglang — through Settings → Providers → Add server: paste an address, click Find models, save. It lands in pi’s models.json, so the pi CLI benefits from the same configuration, and the API key never reaches the browser.

Extensions follow the same philosophy. You can install any pi package by npm name, git URL or local folder, see what it adds before enabling it, and switch individual packages, extensions, skills or pi built-ins on and off. Bundled extensions include pi-web-access, pi-visualize, pi-spec-graph, pi-thinkrail-workflow and pi-todos. Skills are discovered from ~/.pi, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, ~/.copilot and ~/.gemini, plus the project-local equivalents — so an existing Claude Code setup is not wasted.

MCP is supported without the usual footguns: servers come from your mcp.json or from Settings, secrets must be ${VAR} or !command references (pasting credentials into a URL is refused), servers shipped by a repository stay off until you approve exactly what they will run, and any call that may change data asks first — Deny, Allow once, Allow in this chat, Always allow.

Installing it and doing a first task🔗

Get the desktop build from thinkrail.ai (macOS Apple Silicon or Intel, Windows x64, Linux x64/ARM64), or use the CLI:

# macOS, Linux, WSL (and Windows under Git Bash)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash

# Windows PowerShell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex

thinkrail ~/code/my-repo

On Linux, the desktop build is the fussy one: you need glibc 2.38+ and GTK 3 / WebKitGTK 4.1 / Ayatana AppIndicator 3 / librsvg 2, which in practice means Ubuntu 24.04 or newer:

sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 \
  libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2

Then a sane first session looks like this:

  1. Open a repo. If you have none ready, Start a new project creates an empty git repository.
  2. Go to Settings and connect a provider (JetBrains AI or your own key), then pick a default model.
  3. Create a workspace from main and describe the task in one sentence — that description is the first prompt.
  4. Let the agent work. Watch the diff land in the Changes panel; open a terminal if you want to run the tests yourself.
  5. Press Review turn, read the whole change, keep or revert hunks, and send comments back if something is off.
  6. Publish the branch and open a pull request from the top bar. ThinkRail shows the CI checks and the review decision, and lets you mark ready, merge, or delete the remote branch.
  7. Merge or close the PR, and the workspace settles itself.

For spec-driven work, add a fifth step: ask the agent to write or update the SPEC.md of the module it touched, and check the Specs panel to see the graph. After a few tasks, the specs become the thing you read before opening the code.

What it does well🔗

Isolation is real. Worktrees are not a gimmick: they are the only mechanism I have seen that makes parallel agents genuinely safe with a shared repository, without copying the whole repo or inventing a proprietary workspace format.

The agent keeps its memory of intent. Specs plus skills plus a shared plan mean a new session does not restart from zero. The graph keeps context small, and the spec_* tools make the agent responsible for its own documentation.

Nothing is locked in. Apache-2.0, no account, your providers, your ~/.pi, your models.json, your git. You can leave ThinkRail and keep your setup, or run the CLI in a browser over SSH on a remote machine.

The GUI is honest about the agent. Snapshotted diffs, per-hunk review, token cost in the header, resources and subagents visible: you always know what happened, how much it cost, and what is still running.

It is free. The app costs nothing; you pay your model provider, and that is it.

Where it still hurts🔗

It is a 0.x product. Version 0.3.1 at the time of writing (November 2026). Expect rough edges, nightly channels, and features that move between releases. The release notes themselves list caveats — for instance, keep/revert only works on the branch diff, not on the single-turn view, and very large diffs start collapsed.

It is pi-only. ThinkRail is a host for one engine. If your workflow is built around Claude Code, Cursor or Codex, this is not a drop-in replacement — there are community forks experimenting with that, but the official product is deliberately about pi. The bet is that a minimal, extensible harness plus a good GUI beats a monolith.

Linux packaging is the weak spot. Ubuntu 24.04+ effectively, unsigned builds, no notarized macOS CLI. The Windows CLI and desktop binaries are signed, macOS desktop DMGs are signed and notarized, macOS CLI is signed but not notarized. On Linux, expect to verify checksums yourself.

It phones home by default. Launches, chat creation, message sends and provider connections are collected under a random installation ID; error reports are always sent, with the error type and location in ThinkRail’s own code, never prompts or file paths. You can opt out of the additional sharing with thinkrail --no-analytics or THINKRAIL_NO_ANALYTICS=1. It is mild as telemetry goes, but it is on by default, so decide deliberately.

Spec-driven development is a discipline, not a switch. If you and the agent do not maintain the SPEC.md files, the graph becomes archaeology. The tooling helps; it does not replace the habit.

You still have to review. The whole point is to make review cheap, not optional. An agent with a shell, a worktree and merge rights will eventually produce something plausible and wrong; the receipt and the per-hunk review exist precisely because trust must be verified.

Verdict🔗

ThinkRail is the most coherent answer I have seen to a question the industry is still fumbling: what does an IDE look like when the code is written by an agent? Not a chat sidebar glued to the old editor, not a browser sandbox that hides the filesystem, but a workspace manager where the unit of work is an isolated branch, the unit of review is a turn, and the unit of memory is a spec graph.

It is early, it is pi-only, and its Linux packaging will annoy some people. But the ideas are right, the implementation is refreshingly small, and the price — free, open source, no account, bring your own model — makes it a very cheap experiment. If you already live in pi, install it today. If you do not, it is the best excuse I know to try pi.

entry.title: DeepSeek Flash 4.1: the open source model putting pressure on the American players
entry.content:
Let me be blunt: DeepSeek’s latest model, Flash 4.1, kind of blew my mind.

We’re used to DeepSeek shipping solid models at ridiculous prices. But this time, they went one step further, and not a small one.

Open source, for real🔗

The first thing is that Flash 4.1 is open source. Not “half open weights”, not “open but with a license that forbids you from using it for work”. No: the weights are there, you can download them, host them yourself, fine-tune them, run them on your own infra.

That’s a huge difference. When you depend on a closed API, you depend on someone else: their prices, their terms, their outages, their dumb model changes that break your production overnight. Here, you stay in control.

And the price…🔗

That’s the second point, and probably the most annoying one for the competition.

Flash 4.1 costs a fraction of what the American models charge, for a level of quality that, honestly, has little left to envy them for on most everyday tasks. Generating code, writing, summarizing, extracting data, holding a conversation: for 90% of real use cases, the difference has become hard to justify.

When an open, nearly free model does the same job as a closed model billed ten times more, at some point you need a real reason to pay. “It’s a US model” is no longer one.

Real competition for the American models🔗

That’s where it gets interesting. The big American players (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) built their business on two pillars: performance, and being the only ones able to deliver it.

The first pillar still holds, but less and less. The second one is collapsing.

Because DeepSeek’s strategy is brutal: they publish openly, they slash prices, and they force everyone to go back to the drawing board. Other labs now have to either lower their rates or justify added value that no longer exists for most customers. That’s enormous pressure, and it comes from a player that, only a few years ago, wasn’t even in the race.

What it changes for us🔗

Concretely, for someone like me who tinkers with projects, writes scripts, and uses AI to rough out work: it means we can stop counting every token as if it were gold.

We can test, make mistakes, iterate, and re-run generations without it hurting our wallet. We can also host the model ourselves if we have sensitive data and don’t want to send it off to a third-party provider. In short, we get control back.

Fair warning, though🔗

I’m not going to fall into fanboyism either. An open source model means you handle the infra, the updates, the security. It’s not magic. And on the most demanding tasks, the American frontier models still keep a lead.

But for everything else, the question is no longer “is open source good enough?”. The question has become “why would I pay full price for this?”.

In short🔗

Flash 4.1 isn’t just a good model. It’s a signal: quality is becoming commoditized, prices are collapsing, and the closed American models are going to have to learn to live with competition they no longer control.

And honestly, that’s good news for everyone. Except for their margins.

entry.title: From « Code Monkey » to Systemic Orchestrator: how the developer job is changing
entry.content:
For a long time, a developer’s daily life often came down to one thing: turning an idea into lines of code by hand, loop by loop, semicolon by semicolon.

Today, any LLM can generate a function or a UI in three seconds. Typing code by the mile no longer has any value. The job isn’t dead, but its focus is shifting radically.

Less syntax, more judgment🔗

Generating code has become free. Maintaining and understanding it remains costly. Day to day, our time no longer goes into hunting for syntax or boilerplate code, but into three essential topics:

  1. Expressing the need clearly: If the instruction is vague, the AI produces a bad solution in a flash. Precision in modeling and business rules matters more than ever.
  2. Reviewing with a critical eye: Generated code often looks clean at first glance. That’s misleading: edge cases, security holes, or logical nonsense hide easily inside it. Our main role has become that of a ruthless reviewer.
  3. Hardening the tests: To trust code you didn’t type yourself, you need solid tests (unit, integration, strict typing). The test harness becomes our safety net.

The big picture rather than the isolated brick🔗

AI is good at coding one specific function, but it has a short memory and doesn’t see the big picture. Architecture choices, module breakdown, infra cost management, and database consistency remain purely human decisions.

If you let agents stack code without any control, you quickly end up with an unmanageable codebase that nobody masters: tech debt on autopilot.

What about beginners?🔗

That’s probably the real pain point. You used to become senior by breaking things and spending nights hunting for a bug in your own code.

For a junior today, the trap is using AI as a crutch without ever understanding what runs under the hood. The key to learning is shifting: it’s less about writing from a blank page than about learning to read, debug, and challenge what gets generated.

In short🔗

The job doesn’t disappear, it sheds its most mechanical part. Less time wasted on basic plumbing, more energy invested in design, robustness, and value for the user.

entry.title: Alacritty: my everyday terminal ⚡
entry.content:
I do more and more things from the terminal. For that everyday use, I needed an ultra-efficient tool: Alacritty.

Day to day, Alacritty has become indispensable. Written in Rust and GPU-accelerated, it goes straight to the point.

What wins me over:

  • 🛡️ Robustness: Exemplary stability, it never crashes even under heavy load.
  • ⚡ Speed: GPU rendering means instant keystrokes.
  • ⚙️ Simplicity: A minimalistic, clear configuration file.

A must-have when you live in the terminal!

entry.title: Herdr: the terminal multiplexer built for AI agents 🤖
entry.content:
With the rise of AI coding agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor Agent…), the way we work in the terminal is changing fast. Running several agents in parallel inside a classic multiplexer (like tmux or zellij) quickly becomes messy when you need to track who’s doing what. That’s where Herdr comes in.

What is Herdr?🔗

Herdr is a persistent terminal multiplexer built specifically for the age of AI agents. It runs as a background server and adds an agent-aware management layer on top of your usual PTYs.

What Herdr lets you do🔗

  • 🚦 Real-time status tracking: Herdr automatically detects each agent’s state and displays it clearly (running, waiting for input, blocked, or done). No more endless scrolling to figure out whether an agent needs you!
  • 🔄 Absolute persistence: Your tasks keep running even if you close your terminal window or disconnect an SSH session.
  • 🔌 API & automation: Through its CLI and socket API, agents can themselves interact with the multiplexer (open new tabs, launch sub-tasks).
  • 🖥️ Native terminal: It integrates seamlessly with your favorite terminal emulator using standard PTYs.

In short🔗

If you use AI agents in the CLI every day for your projects and want to maximize your productivity without losing track, Herdr is a tool you should try right away.

entry.title: 🚧 Gitlab and Github pages handling the same code 🤓
entry.content:
Hello,

A small trick to have your static website hosted on github + gitlab, with the same source code.

Why ? If one fall of course ! :D And also because it’s fun, at least i think it’s fun :)

Gitlab - Master🔗

  • create our static website repo
  • add web stuff inside the repo
  • configure CI

create our static website repo🔗

let’s pretend our repo name is upcreid.gitlab.io and it’s a hugo static website. Let’s create it and make it public

then the usual stuff:

git clone git@gitlab.com:upcreid/upcreid.gitlab.io.git
cd upcreid.gitlab.io
touch README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "add README"
git push -u origin master

create gh-pages branch🔗

before going further we’ll need to create a gh-pages branch on gitlab side, this in order to not break the CI when pushing without a gh-pages branch.

Go then !

git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git rm --cached -r .
git commit -m "new gh-pages branch" --allow-empty
git push origin gh-pages

go back to master

git checkout master

add web stuff inside the repo🔗

Ok, now let’s add some code inside to have some static shit in there.

  • Install hugo
  • Create new site
hugo new site --force .
  • Install a theme
git submodule add https://github.com/theNewDynamic/gohugo-theme-ananke.git themes/ananke
  • add the theme, name and remove baseURL to the conf file
echo $'languageCode = \"en-us\"\ntitle = \"upcreid.gitlab.io\"\ntheme = \"ananke\"' > config.toml
  • Start the server to verify if everythin goes ok
hugo server
  • Commit
git add .
git commit -m "add basic hugo"
git push

configure CI🔗

Complicated !

Just add one more file to the repo…

.gitlab-ci.yml

image: registry.gitlab.com/pages/hugo:latest

variables:
  GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY: recursive

pages:
  script:
  - hugo -b "https://upcreid.gitlab.io"
  artifacts:
    paths:
    - public
  only:
  - master
  • Commit
git add .
git commit -m "add basic hugo"
git push

and voila => https://upcreid.gitlab.io

Now, let’s handle github.

Github - Mirror🔗

  • create our static website repo
  • branch configuration
  • git mirror
  • configure CI

create our static website repo🔗

Branch configuration🔗

After creation, create a branch called master. To be in phase with gitlab

echo "# upcreid.github.io" >> README.md
git init
git add README.md
git commit -m "first commit"
git branch -M master
git remote add origin git@github.com:upcreid/upcreid.github.io.git
git push -u origin master

Git mirror🔗

Main part of this is to trigger the mirroring on gitlab side. So inside gitlab repo, simply launch

git remote add --mirror=push github git@github.com:upcreid/upcreid.github.io.git

So, we add a remote, and say it’s a mirror (–mirror) and we name it github.

Verify

git remote -v

you should have something like:

github  git@github.com:upcreid/upcreid.github.io.git (fetch)
github  git@github.com:upcreid/upcreid.github.io.git (push)
origin  git@gitlab.com:upcreid/upcreid.gitlab.io.git (fetch)
origin  git@gitlab.com:upcreid/upcreid.gitlab.io.git (push)

configure CI🔗

Then create the github CI file, we’ll use the github actions. But we should commit those github action inside the gitlab repo.

So inside the gitlab repo aka master, create the following dir/file:

mkdir .github/workflows
touch .github/workflows/gh-pages.yml

And inside the gh-pages.yml

name: github pages

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - master

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-18.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
        with:
          submodules: true  # Fetch Hugo themes (true OR recursive)
          fetch-depth: 0    # Fetch all history for .GitInfo and .Lastmod

      - name: Setup Hugo
        uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v2
        with:
          hugo-version: '0.81.0'

      - name: Build
        run: hugo -b "https://upcreid.github.io"

      - name: Deploy
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: ./public

And commit

git add .
git commit -m "add github CI"
git push origin && git push github

As you can see, last command is in fact 2 commands. in order to push on gitlab + github. Some tricks can be made here to push with one command => google

And that’s it => https://upcreid.github.io/

Conclusion🔗

Since you got 2 remote you’ll need to push to those remote after commiting.

you can do that simply with

git push origin && git push github

Then, nothing more should be done and both CI will be triggered.

See you !

entry.title: Git two accounts alias
entry.content:
Hello,

Recently, I was faced with a problem. How to manage two git accounts on the same computer? I explain myself, a “personal” account and a “work” account, on the same computer. Yes, I know that working on personal things with work materials is a bad habit … but that’s another question.

So, to get rid of just that (I did not invent anything, there are a lot of tutorials on the web), you will need to create a separate directory. One for work, one for the person.

Regarding git, you will have to manage your \ $ HOME .gitconfig like this:

[includeIf "gitdir:~/perso/"]
    path = ~/perso/.gitconfig

[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
    path = ~/work/.gitconfig

[user]

So as you see, [user] is not define. So you’ll have to define it in another .gitconfig. So in each directory, create a .gitconfig

in the /perso directory:

[user]
   email = perso@perso.com
   name = name

in the /work directory:

[user]
   email = work@work.com
   name = name

And that’s it. Each time you’ll go into the folder, your “git user” will change.

Bonus🔗

Here is my git alias for log:

yes there is 3, 3 differents view.

[alias]
    lg1 = log --pretty=format:"%C(yellow)%h%Cred%d\\ %Creset%s%Cblue\\ [%cn]" --decorate
    lg2 = log --pretty=format:"%C(yellow)%h%Cred%d\\ %Creset%s%Cblue\\ [%cn]" --decorate --numstat
    l = log --graph --pretty=tformat:'%Cred%h%Creset -%C(yellow)%d%Creset %s %Cgreen(%an %cr)%Creset' --abbrev-commit --date=relative

See you !
